Deploy the landing page and let the harness target a deployment

Live at https://ballast-landing-sepia.vercel.app, production, built by
Vercel from source.

verify.mjs now accepts BASE_URL so the same 35 checks can run against a
deployed build rather than only the local one. That mattered here: the
deployment tool takes file contents inline, so the files were reproduced
by hand rather than uploaded, and behaviour is the only honest way to
confirm the reproduction is faithful.

Verified against production: 35/35 checks passed, and the deployed body
markup is textually identical to the local build once asset hashes are
normalised.

The deployed manifest omits playwright. It is a verification-only dev
dependency whose postinstall downloads browsers, which would slow the
build for no benefit; the page's runtime dependency is gsap alone.

Measure frame timing under CPU throttle

Drives the scroll from requestAnimationFrame and records the interval
between frames, so every ScrollTrigger update runs the way a reader's
scroll would run it. Full page traverse at a 390x844 phone viewport, with
CPU throttle the only variable between runs.

  mode              frames  median     p95   worst   dropped
  unthrottled        205    16.7    17.1    30.3   0 (0.0%)
  4x CPU throttle    205    16.6    17.9    77.0   1 (0.5%)

60fps holds through the whole page at 4x throttle: median 16.6ms, p95
17.9ms, one dropped frame in 205. The 77ms worst case is a single frame
and lines up with the mechanism pin engaging, which is a one-off layout
cost rather than something sustained.

Read as indicative rather than authoritative: headless Chromium is not
vsync-locked to a display, so the shape of the distribution and the
comparison between the two runs carry more weight than absolute fps.

This complements rather than replaces the static check from the beats
commit, that only opacity, x and y are animated and no layout property is.

Count the stakes up, landing exactly on the measured value

Beat 2's three figures now animate. The tween interpolates a proxy object
and formats it for display, never the DOM text node, and on completion the
element is restored to the exact string the build wrote from monitor/data.
A counter that eases into a rounded number and stops there would have
published a wrong figure.

The animated span is aria-hidden and a visually-hidden sibling carries the
real value, so a screen reader reads 739, $27,107,943 and 148 and never
hears the tween. The measured value is also the element's server-rendered
text, so a JavaScript failure leaves the number correct rather than blank.

Expected values in the test are parsed out of the built HTML rather than
typed into the test, so it compares the page against what the build
actually produced.

Verified: npm run build && npm run verify -> 35/35 checks passed, with
counters landing on 739, $27.1M and 148.

The check was proven to have teeth: removing the snap and making the
mid-flight formatter round to the nearest ten drops the run to 33/35 with
'showed 740, authored 739' and 'showed 150, authored 148'. Restored and
re-verified at 35/35 before committing.

Drop Lenis: it broke back/forward scroll restoration

Verification caught a real defect. With Lenis, going back from an in-page
anchor left the reader at scrollY 3362 instead of 0. A control run with
Lenis absent restored to 0 correctly, so the cause was isolated rather
than guessed: Lenis holds its own scroll position and animates back to it
after the browser restores window.scrollY.

Two fixes were tried and measured, and neither worked:

- Resync on popstate fixed back and broke the anchor, freezing its scroll
  at 620px. Instrumenting the page showed why: Chromium fires popstate for
  same-document fragment navigation too, so the handler was interrupting
  the anchor's own scroll.
- Guarding that resync on lenis.isScrolling fixed the anchor and broke
  back again, because the browser's restore scroll makes Lenis report as
  scrolling. The two events are not distinguishable that way.

Back and forward are navigation readers actually use; scroll smoothing is
a feel. ScrollTrigger scrubs and pins identically on native scroll, so the
library went and nothing else changed. The motion chunk drops from 134.80
to 114.87 kB, 50.83 to 45.46 gzip.

Also in this step: nav links to the dashboard, source and enrollment,
which gave keyboard navigation something real to test; a visible
focus-visible outline, since smooth or not, a focused control the reader
cannot see is one they have lost.

Two of the original failures were my tests, not the page. 'target lands
near the top' was wrong because #limits is the last element, so the
browser stops with it 231px down with or without a scroll library; it now
asserts the target is in view. And a fixed 900ms wait was racing the
scroll, so it polls until the position stops changing.

Verified: npm run build && npm run verify -> 29/29 checks passed,
including 'history: back restores the previous position — scrollY 0'.

Verify reduced motion and first paint in a real browser

Turns step 4's static argument into evidence. verify.mjs serves the built
dist over loopback and drives headless chromium, asserting behaviour
rather than reading source.

21/21 checks pass:

- Reduced motion: html class is empty, so Lenis is never constructed. The
  mechanism steps sit at opacity 1 and the hero marker transform is none,
  because the gsap context never executes.
- Motion enabled: html class is lenis, and every figure and caveat is
  already legible at first paint, before any scroll.
- Deep link past the reveal: the drawdown rows read opacity 1,1,1. This
  settles the risk flagged in the previous commit, that gsap.from with
  once:true could leave measured numbers invisible when the page loads
  already scrolled past the trigger. ScrollTrigger fires on refresh.

The checks were proven to have teeth: commenting out the reduced-motion
guard drops the run to 19/21 with 'Lenis never constructed' and 'steps at
full opacity' failing, and the opacities reported as 0.35. Restored and
confirmed identical to HEAD before committing.

Playwright is a dev dependency only and uses a browser already cached on
the machine; nothing was added to the page's runtime dependencies, which
remain gsap and lenis.

Add the scroll beats: hero scrub, drawdown reveal, mechanism pin

Beat 1 puts the product in one gesture: the reader's own scroll drifts a
health factor toward the liquidation line and pulls it back. The floor is
1.04, deliberately above 1.00, because Ballast acts before the seizure
line and showing it dip below would misdescribe the product.

Beat 3 reveals the drawdown rows in table order but holds the -20% row
back so it resolves last and stays emphasised. That row is the argument.

Beat 4 pins the five-step mechanism for exactly one viewport height, well
inside the 1.5 ceiling, and leaves every step legible afterwards so a
reader scrolling back sees the whole transaction rather than four dimmed
boxes.

The hero marker moves by transform, not by left. Its travel is measured
from track layout with invalidateOnRefresh so it survives a resize,
rather than being a hardcoded pixel value.

Verified statically: animated properties are opacity, x and y only, no
layout properties; scrub is 1 in both timelines, never true; pin distance
is +=100%; the reduced-motion guard precedes Lenis construction; teardown
reverts the context, removes the ticker callback, destroys Lenis and kills
every trigger.

Behavioural verification (reduced motion, keyboard, find-in-page, scroll
restoration, throttled framerate) is steps 5, 6 and 8 and needs a browser.

Write the landing content, with every figure derived from monitor/data

data.mjs derives the figures using the same definitions dashboard/build.mjs
uses, then cross-checks its own output against the payload already
embedded in dashboard/index.html and throws on drift. Two surfaces
publishing different numbers for the same measurement is the one failure
this project cannot afford, so it fails the build instead.

Derived, not typed: 739 positions across 676 addresses, $27,107,943 of
debt, 148 positions in the 1.00-1.25 health band, and the drawdown rows
33 / 121 / 192 with $182,701 of penalties at -20%.

Figures are injected at build time by a Vite transformIndexHtml plugin,
so they are in the served HTML and legible with JavaScript disabled. A
counter animation will later replace and restore the visible text, but it
never supplies it. Each figure also carries a visually-hidden exact value
for screen readers.

The stylesheet hides nothing. No opacity:0 or transform offsets on
anything carrying meaning, so reduced motion and no-JS both render the
final state at first paint. Reveal states get set by JS at runtime only.

Beat 5's slippage curve is written qualitatively. Its per-size figures
come from fork-test output rather than monitor/data and have no
machine-readable source yet, so they are not published here.

Verified: node data.mjs -> cross-check matches dashboard; npm run build ->
0 unreplaced tokens; figures and all four caveats present with script tags
stripped; drift guard confirmed to throw by doctoring the dashboard
payload, then restored byte-identical (sha 620a19d22f804bb8).

Add the landing surface, separate from the dashboard

The landing page and the dashboard were the same artifact: vercel.json
sets outputDirectory to dashboard, and there is no landing directory, so
ballast-alpha.vercel.app serves dashboard/index.html. One file cannot
carry both a scroll narrative and a risk tool that must stay readable, so
this splits them.

landing/ is a Vite project with gsap and lenis, following the same
pattern as app/, which Vercel already deploys by root directory. The
dashboard keeps zero dependencies and stays openable from file://.

Measured cost of the motion stack, from vite build:
  motion chunk  134.80 kB raw / 50.83 kB gzip
  app chunk       1.08 kB raw /  0.61 kB gzip

That figure is why the dashboard does not get this. Adding 50 kB gzip of
animation to a 61 kB self-contained page whose value is that its numbers
are checkable is a bad trade.

Lenis rather than ScrollSmoother, and never both: Lenis wraps native
scroll, so sticky, anchors, find-in-page and scroll restoration keep
working. One RAF loop drives Lenis from gsap.ticker so ScrollTrigger
never reads a stale scroll position.

Caveats are static markup from the outset. Not audited, owner powers, and
the ~300k FXRP liquidity ceiling are in the footer, outside any trigger.

Verified: npm run build succeeds; dashboard/ has no changes,
index.html still 61,309 bytes, zero external subresources.

Make the keeper's different-keeper refusal testable

The V3 refusal lived inline in processPolicy using module-level constants
read from the environment at import time, so it could only be verified by
reading the code. Extracted as shouldSkipForDifferentKeeper with identical
semantics and covered by five assertions.

Two behaviours the extraction pins deliberately:

- A policy with no keeper field, which is what a V1-shaped policy looks
  like when read through the V3 ABI, is refused. An unnamed keeper is not
  this operator.
- The check is only reached when EXECUTE is true, because it sits above
  the dry-run return in processPolicy. One test documents that rather than
  changing it, so a dry-run transcript showing no refusal is expected
  behaviour and not evidence the guard is missing.

Stand up a real protected position on Coston2

Bounty 2 now protects something rather than recording verdicts into a
void. Deploys Morpho Blue, an FTSO-backed oracle, tokens and a venue on
Coston2, opens a leveraged position at health 1.1528, and puts it under
confidential protection.

  Morpho Blue          0x5711398A701B9D2BD47Ac8248Cba3A8cA72D053E
  FtsoMorphoOracle     0x3C6379C847Af48e1e33C280Ee00f5D84ae6c02cc
  BallastManagerV2     0x2cC2d9aB9Fca74958C404749C2b9e88C47C6AA70
  ConfidentialTrigger  0x2Ab8F9aac70923DBd375904560e4385e2a2857D7

The oracle is the real FTSOv2 XRP/USD block-latency feed, not a mock: it
returned 1.062995e36 at deployment. That is the point of building the
market rather than faking it, since the whole premise of Ballast is
racing a ~2s oracle.

Verified on-chain: policyOf exposes only a 1.10 ceiling and a salted
commitment, never the real trigger; and protect() from a stranger reverts
NotKeeper (0xcf7d3ecf).

Two traps worth recording. Morpho pins solc 0.8.19 exactly while Ballast
targets ^0.8.26, so no single compiler can import it: MorphoArtifact.sol
is a 0.8.19 shim that forces the artifact to exist for deployCode. And a
hand-rolled IRM with bytes parameters compiles fine, then reverts
createMarket with an unrecognised selector; ZeroIrm now implements
Morpho's own IIrm, selector 0x9451fed4.

The ERC20s and the venue are scaffolding and are documented as such. No
slippage claim rests on them; those come from the mainnet fork tests.

40/40 tests green.

Deploy the confidential trigger to Coston2

Extension registered against the live FlareTeeManager, ID 65962.

  BallastInstructionSender 0x2E9F7A5E62068CAbfafBE83d142cD4b1deeEfdFE
  ConfidentialTrigger      0x966410b0834089A09CcB6E6DE9cB59e9D653598F
  VerdictRecorder          0xB9Eecc16120D18E075eb52198decE2aC22BfD5f6

Coston2 rather than mainnet because Flare split its own stack: Morpho,
FXRP and SparkDEX are on mainnet, where FlareTeeManager has no code and
the contract registry returns zero for it. A contract verifying TEE
signatures has to sit where the registry is.

VerdictRecorder is the honest consequence. It records what
ConfidentialTrigger accepted and returns zeros, because there is no
market on Coston2 to deleverage against and inventing plausible numbers
would be worse than stopping at the boundary of what can be shown.

Its trigger is a one-time setter rather than a constructor arg, since the
trigger and recorder each need the other's address.

40/40 tests green.

Merge the confidential trigger for Bounty 2

Brings in the Flare Confidential Compute work alongside the live Bounty 1
deployment. Additive only: BallastManager.sol and SparkDexAdapter.sol are
untouched, so the contracts deployed at 0x379e...5571 and 0x62a7...E8b1
still match their verified source.

- TeeResultHash.sol reproduces the three-keccak digest a TEE machine
  signs, pinned to a fixture generated from Flare's own Go code
- ConfidentialTrigger.sol accepts a verdict only from a machine the Flare
  registry says runs our extension in PRODUCTION
- BallastManagerV2.sol adds the keeper gate and clamps verdict parameters
  to the borrower's own policy
- fce/ is the Go extension, driven end to end against a live mainnet
  position with its health math bracketed against the deployed contract

40/40 Solidity tests and the Go tests green.

Fix three bugs found by running the extension for real

Ran the extension inside a scaffold clone with a mock sign sidecar
against live Flare mainnet state. Unit tests had passed throughout; all
three of these only appear when a real instruction arrives.

- decodeTuple round-tripped through JSON. geth decodes bytes32 to
  [32]byte, which marshals as an array of numbers, so every instruction
  failed to decode. Use abi.ConvertType instead.
- Request struct fields must match geth's abi.ToCamelCase output.
  MarketID does not bind to marketId; MarketId does.
- The chain reader's Morpho address was never set, so every read would
  have gone to the zero address. Wired through MORPHO_ADDRESS.

Full ENROLL -> EVALUATE -> verdict now works on the real ~$83k position,
and the verdict ABI-decodes to exactly ConfidentialTrigger.Verdict.

The enclave's health math is bracketed against the chain: healthOf
reported 1150998153316783502, a secret trigger of 1.150e18 produced no
verdict and 1.152e18 produced one. The Go reimplementation of Morpho's
share accounting agrees with the deployed Solidity.

Also records that the scaffold's main pins tee-node below the v0.0.22
minimum Flare specifies, which silently empties the vote queue.

Add the Ballast Flare Compute Extension

The Go extension that holds the secret trigger, plus the InstructionSender
that is the only address allowed to instruct it.

ENROLL takes a policy encrypted to the machine's public key, decrypts it
through the tee-node sign sidecar, checks it hashes to the commitment the
borrower published on-chain, and holds the plaintext in enclave memory
only. That commitment check is what makes the on-chain hash mean
anything: without it a borrower could publish one policy and run a
different one.

EVALUATE reads the Morpho position and oracle price at a block pinned in
the request, computes health with Morpho's own share accounting, and
returns an ABI-encoded verdict only when the secret trigger is crossed.
A 'nothing to do' answer is success with an empty payload, so the caller
never learns how far from the trigger a position sits.

GET /state exposes aggregate counters only. It is observable outside the
enclave, so per-borrower detail there would hand back the secret.

Go and Solidity are pinned to hash a policy identically by fixtures on
both sides, since a divergence would reject every enrollment with an
error that explains nothing.

go build and go test pass; 40/40 Solidity tests green. Not yet run inside
a real tee-node.

Add BallastManagerV2 with the keeper gate and verdict clamping

v1's protect() is permissionless, so a searcher could bypass the enclave
entirely by calling it directly the moment they saw a position enrolled.
v2 adds an optional Policy.keeper: when set, only that address may act.

protectFor() lets the enclave supply target health and slippage, but
clamps both to the borrower's on-chain policy rather than trusting them.
A compromised enclave can at worst do something the borrower already
authorised. Lower-than-policy values pass through, since acting more
conservatively than authorised is always safe.

Corrects a design error found by the tests: I had planned to set the
public trigger permissively high and the target below it, which violates
v1's targetHealth > triggerHealth invariant and would have left every
protected position instantly re-armed. The trigger is now a public
ceiling with the secret trigger below it, so the leak drops from an exact
value to a band. Documented as such rather than oversold.

39/39 tests green, 8 of them new fork tests against a real position.

Pin the TEE result digest against Flare's own Go implementation

My first cut signed keccak256(abi.encode(verdict)), which was wrong and
would have rejected every real verdict on-chain while passing every unit
test. The actual chain a TEE machine signs is three keccak rounds:

  dataHash = keccak256(keccak256(data) || id || keccak256(tag) || status)
  signHash = keccak256(abi.encode(bytes32("TEE_ACTION_RESULT"), chainId, dataHash))
  digest   = keccak256(signHash)

The third round is easy to miss: Wallet.Sign takes a message, not a
digest, so it hashes again before crypto.Sign. The domain separator binds
a signature to both its purpose and its chain.

TeeResultHash is asserted against a fixture generated by running Flare's
Go code, including recovering a real geth signature on-chain, so a change
upstream fails loudly here instead of silently in production.

31/31 tests green.

Add the confidential trigger verifier for Flare Confidential Compute

Bounty 2. Ballast v1 stores Policy.triggerHealth in public storage, so a
searcher can read every protected position's exact trip wire. This moves
the trigger behind a commitment and puts the decision inside a TEE.

On-chain trust comes from Flare's machine registry rather than a
hardcoded key: a verdict is only accepted if ecrecover yields a machine
that getExtensionId says runs our extension and getTeeMachineStatus says
is in PRODUCTION.

Three constraints found by reading the live chain rather than the docs:
instruction payloads are public in the TeeInstructionsSent event, so the
trigger must be encrypted to the machine key from getPublicKey; results
never return on-chain by themselves, so a keeper relays a signed verdict;
and evaluation must be pinned to a block or machines disagree on result
bytes.

24/24 tests green.

Make the dashboard deployable with zero configuration

- vercel.json serves dashboard/ as a static site with no build step, so
  importing the repo needs no settings.
- dashboard/build.mjs now falls back to the published data snapshot in this
  repo when monitor/data is absent, so a host with only the dashboard
  directory can regenerate the page. Verified byte-identical to a local
  build (sha256 ea9885f1...).
- Compact the wire format: intern the repeated venue and market strings and
  emit rows as tuples, deriving the liquidation parameters from the venue
  rather than repeating them per row. The page drops from 105KB to 58KB with
  identical figures.

Truncate borrower addresses in the published data and dashboard

These positions are public on-chain state that anyone can recompute, but a
ranked list of who is closest to liquidation is directly useful to a
liquidation bot, and publishing one is a different act from the data merely
existing on chain. Aggregates are unaffected.

- monitor/redact.mjs truncates borrower addresses in the result snapshots.
  It widens a label rather than collapsing two distinct addresses onto one,
  so counts of unique addresses stay exact: 475 and 303 distinct borrowers
  map to 475 and 303 labels with no collisions.
- Drop monitor/data/accounts.json from the repo and ignore it. It is a
  scanner intermediate holding 2,516 raw addresses with no analytical value;
  the enosys scan regenerates it locally.
- Dashboard renders whatever label it is given and no longer reveals a full
  address on hover. The page now carries zero 40-hex addresses.
- Note the policy in the README and in the page footer.

Headline figures are unchanged: 739 positions, 676 unique addresses,
$27,107,943 of debt.

Full addresses remain in the fork tests, where they are functionally
required to read real positions from mainnet.

Ballast: automated deleveraging for XRP collateral on Flare

Protects leveraged FXRP positions from liquidation by repaying part of the
debt out of collateral before the liquidation line is crossed, spending a
swap fee to avoid a ~7.4% liquidation penalty.

Contracts
- BallastManager: non-custodial policy registry plus flash-loan deleverage.
  The borrower authorises Ballast on Morpho and sets their own bounds
  (trigger/target health, max collateral per action, max slippage, keeper
  fee ceiling, cooldown). A keeper decides when; the policy decides what is
  permitted.
- SparkDexAdapter: swaps directly against the pool rather than through the
  unverified router, and serves Algebra Integral and Uniswap-V3 pools with
  one implementation.
- HealthMath: health and deleverage sizing using Morpho's own share
  accounting, so 1.00 is exactly the seizure line.
- SafeTransfer: USDT-family tokens may not return a bool.

Evidence
- Scanners measure the real market: 739 XRP-collateralised positions across
  676 addresses, $27.1M debt against $57.0M collateral, on Morpho Blue and
  the Enosys isolated markets. An XRP -20% move liquidates 121 positions and
  destroys roughly $183K in penalties.
- Dashboard renders that dataset as a self-contained page.

Tests (14, forked at a pinned block against live mainnet state)
- Real borrower positions are read and rescued, including one already below
  the liquidation line at XRP -20%.
- Measured slippage: selling FXRP costs 65bps at 1k and 1807bps at 500k, so
  deleveraging only beats liquidation up to roughly 300k FXRP per sale.
- A faithful drawdown moves the pool as well as the oracle; the same trade
  then costs ~4.8% instead of ~1.2%, and a bound calibrated on a calm pool
  correctly refuses to fire.

Known gaps: not deployed to a public network, no keeper running, single-venue
routing, and policies are still public on-chain rather than held in a TEE.
